title: Single-Address-Space FaaS with Jord
problem: Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) systems incur millisecond-level overheads from isolating functions in separate address spaces (containers or microVMs), preventing them from meeting microsecond-scale service-level objectives (SLOs) required by microservice workloads. The address-space isolation mechanism forces costly context switches, copy-on-write, and cross-function data copies.
motivation: FaaS was designed for microsecond-level event-driven execution, but all modern implementations impose container/VM overhead that pushes latency to milliseconds — a 1000x gap from the intended design point — limiting the paradigm's usefulness for latency-sensitive microservices.
method: Jord co-locates functions in a single memory space but isolates them using hardware memory protection keys—CPU features that mark which memory regions each function can access, with enforcement at nanosecond speed and no OS involvement required. Functions share memory directly without copying, and Jord's scheduler switches between functions within the process instead of triggering OS context switches. The result is microsecond-scale latency instead of the millisecond overhead of container isolation.
key_novelty: Jord achieves microsecond-scale function latency by co-locating functions in a single memory space with hardware-enforced isolation at nanosecond granularity, instead of isolating them in separate containers or virtual machines.
contributions: A single-address-space FaaS architecture with user-level in-process memory isolation that operates at nanosecond granularity.
Zero-copy cross-function communication enabled by colocation in a shared address space with hardware-enforced isolation.
Demonstration that Jord meets microsecond-level SLOs while performing within 16% of an idealized but insecure baseline.
Over 2x higher throughput compared to enhanced state-of-the-art FaaS systems.

metrics.speedup: Over 2x throughput vs. enhanced state-of-the-art FaaS
metrics.other: Within 16% of idealized insecure baseline; microsecond-level SLO achieved

limitations: Not discussed; security properties of user-level memory isolation under adversarial function code are not thoroughly analyzed.
primary_theme: Single-address-space FaaS with user-level in-process memory isolation
